scenes.title: Abraham welcomes the visitors and Sarah hears the promise

art.alt: Abraham serves three seated visitors beneath a tree, while Sarah listens from the open tent entrance; artistic reconstruction

scenes.caption: Illustrated reconstruction · Genesis 18:1–15

intro.title: Visitors at Mamre
intro.note: Genesis 18:1 introduces Abraham at the tent door in Mamre. The illustration gathers the welcome, meal, and Sarah hearing the promise into a single editorial scene. It does not establish the appearance of these people or a precise campsite.

hotspots.title: Abraham welcomes the visitors
hotspots.note: Abraham runs to meet the three men and offers water, rest, and food. The visible visitors help explain the welcome described in Genesis 18:2–5.

hotspots.title: Abraham serves the meal
hotspots.note: Sarah prepares cakes, a young man prepares the calf, and Abraham serves butter, milk, and the prepared calf beneath the tree. He stands by the visitors while they eat.

detail.alt: Close view of bread cakes, a milk vessel, butter, and prepared meat on a woven cloth; artistic reconstruction

hotspots.title: Sarah hears the promise
hotspots.note: Sarah hears from the tent door that she will have a son. She laughs within herself because of their age, and the Lord questions her response. The doorway matters because she listens there.

scenes.title: The pledge Judah gives

art.alt: A stone signet, braided bracelets, and a wooden staff arranged on cloth; reconstructed forms of the pledge objects named in Genesis

scenes.caption: Illustrated object study · Genesis 38:18 · Object forms are reconstructed

intro.title: Judah's pledge
intro.note: Genesis names the objects Judah gives as a pledge. The exact design and materials are reconstructed.

hotspots.title: The pledge that identifies Judah
hotspots.note: Tamar asks for Judah’s signet, bracelets, and staff as a pledge. Later, these objects identify him. This object study illustrates their role without depicting the encounter described in the verse.

detail.alt: The signet, bracelets, and wooden staff shown together as a reconstructed object study

scenes.title: Judah recognizes the pledge

art.alt: The pledge objects are presented to Judah, who responds with recognition; artistic reconstruction of the recognition episode

scenes.caption: Illustrated reconstruction · Genesis 38:25–26

intro.title: Recognizing the evidence
intro.note: The returned pledge objects connect the accusation with Judah's earlier promise. The staging of this scene is an artistic reconstruction.

hotspots.title: Tamar sends the evidence
hotspots.note: Tamar sends word to Judah, asking him to recognize the signet, bracelets, and staff. These are the objects he gave as a pledge earlier in the chapter.

detail.alt: Detail of the reconstructed signet, bracelets, and staff that identify the pledge

hotspots.title: Judah acknowledges his failure
hotspots.note: Judah recognizes the objects and acknowledges his failure to give Tamar to Shelah his son. The illustration focuses on his recognition and admission.

scenes.title: Israel crosses on dry ground between divided waters

art.alt: Moses and Israelites cross the exposed seabed between walls of water; artistic reconstruction

scenes.caption: Illustrated reconstruction · Exodus 14:21–29 · not a geographic map or verified modern site

intro.title: Crossing on dry ground
intro.note: Exodus says the waters divide and Israel crosses on dry ground, with the waters as a wall on either side. This illustration represents that passage and does not establish a surveyed location or modern route.

hotspots.title: Israel crosses between the divided waters
hotspots.note: Exodus 14:21–29 describes the LORD making the sea dry land, the children of Israel entering into the midst of the sea on dry ground, and the waters standing as a wall on both sides. The hotspot focuses on the crossing.

scenes.title: Aaron lays his hands on the live goat

art.alt: Aaron lays both hands on the live goat as an attendant prepares to lead it toward the wilderness; artistic reconstruction

scenes.caption: Illustrated reconstruction · Leviticus 16:20–22

intro.title: The live goat
intro.note: Leviticus 16:21–22 says Aaron lays both hands on the live goat's head, confesses Israel's iniquities, and sends it with a fit man into the wilderness. The image illustrates that passage; it does not claim an exact historical setting or appearance.

hotspots.title: Aaron lays his hands on the live goat
hotspots.note: Aaron lays both his hands upon the head of the live goat and confesses over it the iniquities of Israel. A fit man is to send the goat away into the wilderness (Leviticus 16:21–22).

scenes.title: Balaam, the donkey, and the angel

art.alt: A donkey beside a vineyard wall, Balaam bowing, and a messenger holding a drawn sword in the narrow path; artistic reconstruction

scenes.caption: Illustrated reconstruction · Numbers 22:21–35 · Appearance and setting are illustrative

intro.title: Balaam, the donkey, and the angel
intro.note: The donkey sees the angel before Balaam does. This single illustration brings together the encounter’s adjacent moments; it is not an ancient map.

hotspots.title: The donkey turns aside from the sword
hotspots.note: The donkey sees the angel with a drawn sword, turns aside, and presses against the wall before falling down. Balaam strikes it because he does not yet see what it sees.

hotspots.title: The donkey speaks to Balaam
hotspots.note: The LORD opens the donkey’s mouth. It asks Balaam why he has struck it, and he answers. The image identifies the speaking animal without adding words to Scripture.

hotspots.title: Balaam sees the angel blocking the way
hotspots.note: Balaam’s eyes are opened, and he sees the angel with the drawn sword. He bows and is instructed to speak only the word given to him. The messenger’s appearance is reconstructed.

scenes.title: Moses calls Israel to choose life

art.alt: Moses addresses seated listeners under an open sky; the people and setting are artistically reconstructed

scenes.caption: Illustrated reconstruction · Deuteronomy 30:15–20 · Appearance and setting are illustrative

intro.title: Moses calls Israel to choose life
intro.note: Moses places a choice before Israel through his words. The illustration shows the speaker and hearers, without turning life and death into invented geographic routes.

hotspots.title: Moses sets life and good before Israel
hotspots.note: Moses sets life and good against death and evil. He calls Israel to love the LORD, walk in his ways, and keep his commandments. The visible speaker represents this address.

hotspots.title: Israel hears the warning against turning away
hotspots.note: Moses warns what will follow if Israel turns away to serve other gods. The listeners stand for those addressed; their presence does not depict them rejecting the warning.

hotspots.title: Moses calls heaven and earth as witnesses
hotspots.note: Moses calls heaven and earth to record the choice and urges Israel to choose life, love the LORD, obey his voice, and cleave to him. The raised hand and sky illustrate his address.

scenes.title: The priests stand in the Jordan as Israel crosses

art.alt: Priests carry the gold-overlaid Ark with a gold mercy seat and paired cherubim while Israelites cross; artistic reconstruction based on Exodus 25:10–22

scenes.caption: Illustrated reconstruction · Joshua 3:14–17; Ark details based on Exodus 25:10–22 · not a verified modern site

intro.title: The crossing of the Jordan
intro.note: Joshua 3:14–17 describes priests bearing the Ark standing firm on dry ground in the midst of the Jordan while the Israelites pass over. The Ark is depicted as an artistic reconstruction using the gold overlay, mercy seat, and paired cherubim described in Exodus 25:10–22; no modern crossing location is identified.

hotspots.title: The priests stand with the Ark in the river
hotspots.note: The priests bearing the Ark of the covenant stand firm on dry ground in the midst of the Jordan until all the people have passed over (Joshua 3:14–17).

scenes.title: Deborah speaks with Barak beneath the palm

art.alt: Deborah addresses Barak beneath a palm tree as a few people wait nearby; artistic reconstruction

scenes.caption: Illustrated reconstruction · Judges 4:4–10

intro.title: Deborah and Barak
intro.note: Judges 4:4–10 identifies Deborah as a prophetess who judged Israel beneath her palm tree, and describes her calling Barak and going with him. This illustration depicts their conversation without claiming a precise historical appearance or place.

hotspots.title: Deborah calls Barak
hotspots.note: Deborah sends and calls Barak, tells him the LORD has commanded him to gather men, and agrees to go with him (Judges 4:5–9).

scenes.title: Boaz welcomes Ruth to glean among the reapers

art.alt: Boaz speaks with Ruth in a barley field as she gleans among the reapers; artistic reconstruction

scenes.caption: Illustrated reconstruction · Ruth 2:8–17

intro.title: Ruth gleans in Boaz's field
intro.note: Ruth 2:8–17 describes Boaz telling Ruth to remain with his maidens, drink from the vessels, and glean among the sheaves; he instructs his workers to leave grain for her. The illustration represents one encounter in the field and does not establish property boundaries or a precise location.

hotspots.title: Boaz tells Ruth to stay with his workers
hotspots.note: Boaz tells Ruth to glean with his maidens and commands his workers to leave handfuls of grain for her (Ruth 2:8–9, 15–16).

scenes.title: David advances toward Goliath with his sling

art.alt: Unarmored young David advances with a sling toward the armored Goliath and his shield-bearer; artistic reconstruction

scenes.caption: Illustrated reconstruction · 1 Samuel 17:40–50 · the scene shows the approach before the strike

intro.title: David faces Goliath
intro.note: First Samuel 17:40–50 tells how David, carrying a sling and stones, runs toward the approaching Philistine and prevails with a sling and a stone. This illustration shows the tense approach before the strike, not the blow or its aftermath.

hotspots.title: David approaches with his sling
hotspots.note: David takes his sling and stones and draws near to the Philistine; Goliath approaches with a shield-bearer before him. The scene focuses on the moment before their encounter (1 Samuel 17:40–41, 48).

scenes.title: David dances before the Ark as it enters Jerusalem

art.alt: David dances as the gold-overlaid Ark is carried in procession, with Michal watching from one distant window; compressed artistic reconstruction

scenes.caption: Compressed illustrated reconstruction · 2 Samuel 6:12–23 · no city layout implied

intro.title: The Ark enters Jerusalem
intro.note: Second Samuel 6 describes the Ark's procession, David dancing before the LORD, and Michal watching from a window. This compressed illustration places those textual details in one editorial scene; it does not reconstruct Jerusalem's layout. The Ark's gold overlay and cherubim are an artistic reconstruction following Exodus 25:10–22.

hotspots.title: David dances before the Ark
hotspots.note: David dances before the LORD as the Ark is brought up with shouting and the sound of the trumpet (2 Samuel 6:12–15).

hotspots.title: Michal watches from the window
hotspots.note: Michal sees David leaping and dancing before the LORD from a window and later speaks with him when he returns to bless his household (2 Samuel 6:16, 20–23).

scenes.title: The cloud fills the house of the LORD

art.alt: Priests withdraw as a cloud fills the sanctuary; Levite musicians with trumpet and cymbals stand near the Ark; artistic reconstruction

scenes.caption: Illustrated reconstruction · 1 Kings 8:10–11 · interior layout is not historical documentation

intro.title: The cloud fills the house
intro.note: First Kings 8:10–11 says that when the priests came out of the holy place, the cloud filled the house of the LORD and the priests could not stand to minister. Musicians are included because the same dedication account in 2 Chronicles 5 describes Levite singers and instruments; the interior is an artistic reconstruction, not a documented temple plan.

hotspots.title: The cloud fills the house of the LORD
hotspots.note: The priests come out of the holy place; the cloud fills the house of the LORD, and the priests cannot stand to minister because of the cloud (1 Kings 8:10–11).

scenes.title: Naaman washes in the Jordan at Elisha's word

art.alt: Naaman begins washing in a river while an attendant and Elisha's messenger stand on the bank; compressed artistic reconstruction

scenes.caption: Compressed illustrated reconstruction · 2 Kings 5:9–14 · no modern river location implied

intro.title: Naaman washes in the Jordan
intro.note: Second Kings 5:9–14 tells how Elisha's messenger gives Naaman the instruction to wash in Jordan seven times, his servants encourage him, and he dips himself and is clean. The image compresses these ordered moments into an educational scene; it does not claim an exact location or ritual detail.

hotspots.title: Elisha's messenger gives the instruction
hotspots.note: Elisha sends a messenger with the instruction that Naaman wash in Jordan seven times (2 Kings 5:9–10).

hotspots.title: Naaman's servants urge him to follow the instruction
hotspots.note: Naaman's servants reason with him and encourage him to do as the prophet said (2 Kings 5:13).

hotspots.title: Naaman dips in the Jordan and is made clean
hotspots.note: Naaman dips himself seven times in Jordan according to the word of the man of God; his flesh comes again and he is clean (2 Kings 5:14).

scenes.title: Levites carry the Ark as David celebrates

art.alt: Levites carry the gold-overlaid Ark as David dances and Michal watches from one distant window; compressed artistic reconstruction

scenes.caption: Compressed illustrated reconstruction · 1 Chronicles 15:25–29 · shared event art, no city layout implied

intro.title: The Ark procession
intro.note: First Chronicles 15:25–29 describes the Levites bearing the Ark, David's celebration with singers and instruments, and Michal seeing him from a window. The same procession is illustrated in the 2 Samuel scene; this compressed reconstruction does not imply a precise city layout.

hotspots.title: The Levites carry the Ark with rejoicing
hotspots.note: The Levites bear the Ark while David, the singers, and the people celebrate with trumpets, cymbals, psalteries, and harps (1 Chronicles 15:25–28).

hotspots.title: Michal watches David from the window
hotspots.note: Michal sees King David dancing and playing before the LORD from a window (1 Chronicles 15:29).

scenes.title: Levite musicians praise as the cloud fills the temple

art.alt: Priests withdraw as the cloud fills the sanctuary; Levite musicians sound a trumpet and cymbals beside the Ark; artistic reconstruction

scenes.caption: Illustrated reconstruction · 2 Chronicles 5:11–14 · interior layout is not historical documentation

intro.title: The cloud fills the house of God
intro.note: Second Chronicles 5:11–14 describes the priests, Levite singers, instruments, Ark, and cloud filling the house. The image is shared with the corresponding 1 Kings dedication event and does not claim a documented temple plan.

hotspots.title: The cloud fills the house as the musicians praise
hotspots.note: The Levite singers and 120 priests sound instruments as one in praise; the house is filled with a cloud, and the priests cannot stand to minister (2 Chronicles 5:11–14).

scenes.title: The returned families lay the temple foundation

art.alt: Builders set a stone foundation as priests sound trumpets, Levites play cymbals, and people show both grief and joy; artistic reconstruction

scenes.caption: Artistic reconstruction · Ezra 3:8–13 · temple design unspecified

intro.title: A foundation and mixed voices
intro.note: Ezra describes the work of laying the temple foundation and the people’s mixed response, but gives no reconstructable plan or architectural measurements. The buildings and foundation here are generic artistic reconstruction, not a historical site rendering.

hotspots.title: Builders begin the house’s foundation
hotspots.note: The returned community organizes the work. As the builders lay the foundation, priests with trumpets and Levites with cymbals praise the LORD (Ezra 3:8–10).

hotspots.title: Joy and grief rise together
hotspots.note: The people shout with joy, while older priests, Levites, and family heads who saw the first house weep; the sounds mingle (Ezra 3:11–13).

scenes.title: Families rebuild the wall while keeping watch

art.alt: Builders repair an unfinished wall as armed guards and a trumpet signaler keep watch with Nehemiah; artistic reconstruction

scenes.caption: Illustrated reconstruction · Nehemiah 4:15–23 · no wall plan implied

intro.title: Work and watch
intro.note: Nehemiah 4:15–23 describes the people returning to work, some holding weapons while others build, a trumpet signal for gathering, and a night guard arrangement. The illustration does not show an attack or reconstruct a precise wall layout.

hotspots.title: Builders keep a weapon at hand
hotspots.note: The builders work with one hand while holding a weapon in the other, with swords at their sides (Nehemiah 4:15–18).

hotspots.title: Nehemiah organizes the watch
hotspots.note: The trumpet signals people to gather, and workers lodge within Jerusalem so they can guard at night and labor by day (Nehemiah 4:19–23).

scenes.title: Esther names Haman at the banquet

art.alt: Esther names Haman as the king returns and Haman pleads beside her couch; artistic reconstruction

scenes.caption: Compressed illustrated reconstruction · Esther 7:1–8 · room arrangement unspecified

intro.title: The second banquet
intro.note: Esther 7:1–8 describes Esther identifying Haman and the king returning from the garden as Haman pleads beside Esther's couch. This compressed illustration does not claim a palace room plan or depict physical assault. The narrative continues with Haman's execution in verses 9–10, which is not shown here.

hotspots.title: Esther identifies Haman
hotspots.note: When the king asks who threatens Esther and her people, she identifies Haman as the adversary and enemy (Esther 7:1–6).

hotspots.title: The king returns as Haman pleads
hotspots.note: Haman stands to plead for his life; when the king returns from the garden, he finds Haman by the bed where Esther reclines and interprets what he sees as an assault (Esther 7:7–8). The illustration shows pleading without physical contact.

scenes.title: Job hears questions from the whirlwind

art.alt: Job listens before a non-personified whirlwind as waves meet the shore; poetic illustration

scenes.caption: Poetic landscape illustration · Job 38:1–11 · literary frame, location unspecified

intro.title: Questions from the whirlwind
intro.note: Job 38 uses poetic questions about the earth, morning stars, and the sea’s limits. This illustration treats the book as a literary frame and does not claim a datable location or depict God as a human or angel.

hotspots.title: Job listens as the speech asks about creation
hotspots.note: The speech begins from the whirlwind and asks Job where he was when the earth’s foundation was laid; it also evokes the morning stars (Job 38:1–7).

hotspots.title: The poem gives the sea a boundary
hotspots.note: The poem pictures the sea as emerging from the womb and being bounded by doors and bars, a limit beyond human control (Job 38:8–11).

scenes.title: The shepherd leads and prepares a table

art.alt: A shepherd leads sheep beside still water while a speaker sits beside a prepared table with bread, an overflowing cup, and oil vessel; poetic illustration

scenes.caption: Poetic image · Psalm 23:1–6 · no specific journey or landscape claimed

intro.title: The shepherd and the table
intro.note: Psalm 23 uses shepherding, safe passage, and hospitality as poetic images of the LORD’s care. This illustration is not a reconstruction of one historical journey, location, or literal divine appearance.

hotspots.title: The shepherd leads beside still waters
hotspots.note: The speaker describes the LORD as a shepherd who provides, leads beside still waters, restores the soul, and guides in right paths (Psalm 23:1–3).

hotspots.title: A table and overflowing cup express welcome
hotspots.note: The poem holds danger and welcome together: a table is prepared in the presence of enemies, the speaker is anointed, and the cup overflows (Psalm 23:4–6).

scenes.title: Wisdom calls aloud in the public places

art.alt: A woman representing poetic Wisdom calls at a town gate as some listeners turn toward her and another passes by

scenes.caption: Literary personification · Proverbs 1:20–33 · no historical woman or city claimed

intro.title: Wisdom calls in public
intro.note: Proverbs personifies Wisdom as a woman speaking in the streets and at the gates. This is a teaching poem; the figure is not identified as a historical individual, and the warnings are not depicted as a literal event.

hotspots.title: Wisdom calls to the inexperienced
hotspots.note: The poem places Wisdom’s call in the streets, busy gathering places, and openings of the gates; she urges listeners to turn at her reproof (Proverbs 1:20–23).

hotspots.title: The poem contrasts refusal with listening
hotspots.note: Wisdom says some refuse her counsel, then contrasts the consequences of that refusal with the security of one who listens. The image shows a passerby continuing on, not the poem’s warnings as literal events (Proverbs 1:24–33).

scenes.title: The preacher names a time for every purpose

art.alt: A symbolic montage pairs planting with uprooting and mourning with dancing, while a worker pauses beside finished masonry and an open scroll; literary illustration

scenes.caption: Literary montage · Ecclesiastes 3:1–14 · no single historical episode claimed

intro.title: A time for every purpose
intro.note: Ecclesiastes 3 lists changing seasons of human action and then asks what profit labor gives. These vignettes are literary illustrations rather than one event; the open scroll is a reading cue with no quoted text.

hotspots.title: The poem pairs planting, uprooting, mourning, and dancing
hotspots.note: The poem names contrasting seasons, including planting and uprooting, weeping and laughter, mourning and dancing, without saying people control their timing (Ecclesiastes 3:1–8).

hotspots.title: The preacher asks what lasting profit labor gives
hotspots.note: The seated worker and open scroll frame the preacher’s question about labor and his reflection on human toil, daily enjoyment, and the enduring work of God (Ecclesiastes 3:9–14).

scenes.title: The beloved hears her lover call in spring

art.alt: The beloved looks through a wooden lattice toward her lover beyond a low wall amid spring flowers; literary illustration of poetic speakers, not a documented couple.

scenes.caption: Literary illustration · Song of Solomon 2:8–14 · The poetic speakers are not identified as a historical couple.

intro.title: A spring invitation
intro.note: The poem gives the beloved and her lover speaking voices. The lattice, wall, flowers, vine, and fig leaves draw on its seasonal imagery; faces, clothing, and dwelling details are artistic reconstruction. The scene leaves the speakers’ identities and interpretation open.

hotspots.title: The beloved hears her lover at the lattice
hotspots.note: The beloved describes her lover standing behind the wall and showing himself through the lattice. The image gives the poetic speakers visual form but does not identify them as a dated or documented couple.

hotspots.title: The lover calls her into spring
hotspots.note: The lover invites her to rise and come away as winter passes and flowers, birds, vines, and figs mark spring. The seasonal details are poetic, not a claim about a specific calendar or place.

scenes.title: A shoot from Jesse and a vision of peace

art.alt: A small shoot grows from a stump as a child stands with a ruler and calm predator and prey animals on a hillside; prophetic vision, not a documentary scene

scenes.caption: Prophetic vision · Isaiah 11:1–9 · Literary imagery, not a documentary landscape.

intro.title: A shoot from Jesse and a vision of peace
intro.note: Isaiah 11:1–5 describes a shoot from Jesse and a ruler who judges with righteousness; verses 6–9 picture peace among creatures. This image combines those parts of one oracle. The ruler is an open literary representation, and the animals’ peaceful proximity is prophetic imagery rather than an observed encounter or fixed end-times reading.

hotspots.title: A shoot from Jesse and a righteous ruler
hotspots.note: The oracle begins with a rod and branch from Jesse’s line and describes judgment marked by righteousness and faithfulness. The shoot at the stump illustrates the branch; the nearby adult is a literary rendering, not an identified historical portrait.

hotspots.title: Predator and prey rest together in the vision
hotspots.note: Isaiah pictures the wolf with the lamb, the leopard with the young goat, and other creatures at peace, with a child among them. The scene is explicitly prophetic imagery, not a documented real encounter.

scenes.title: Jeremiah at the potter’s house

art.alt: A potter shapes a clay vessel at a wheel while Jeremiah watches nearby; reconstructed workshop and objects

scenes.caption: Illustrated reconstruction · Jeremiah 18:1–6 · Appearance and setting are illustrative

intro.title: Jeremiah at the potter’s house
intro.note: Jeremiah watches a potter rework a vessel, and the following words explain the clay comparison. The workshop is an illustration, not a recovered historic location.

hotspots.title: The potter remakes the marred vessel
hotspots.note: The vessel is marred in the potter’s hand, so he makes it again into another vessel. His hands and the clay identify the action Jeremiah observes; the wheel’s design is reconstructed.

hotspots.title: Jeremiah hears the comparison to clay
hotspots.note: The LORD asks whether he can do with the house of Israel as this potter does. The clay in the potter’s hand is the passage’s comparison; the image does not settle every later application.

scenes.title: The city sits alone like a widow

art.alt: A grieving woman sits alone on a stone threshold beside a deserted street, a small figure turned away in the distance; literary personification of Daughter Zion, not a historical portrait

scenes.caption: Literary personification · Lamentations 1:1–3 · Daughter Zion as a grieving widow, not a historical portrait.

intro.title: A city rendered as a lone widow
intro.note: Lamentations 1:1–3 compares the once-populous city to a widow and describes tears, abandonment, and exile. The woman is the poem’s personification, not an identified historical person or archaeological reconstruction.

hotspots.title: The city sits alone like a widow
hotspots.note: The opening verse says the city that was full of people now sits alone, like a widow. The seated figure illustrates that comparison.

hotspots.title: The mourner weeps without comfort
hotspots.note: The poem says she weeps and finds no comforter, then describes Judah’s captivity. The outstretched hand echoes the plea for comfort; it is an illustrative gesture, not a separate event.

scenes.title: Ezekiel sees the breath enter and the company stand

art.alt: Ezekiel gestures toward a clothed company standing in a valley as wind moves their garments; a few dry bones lie nearby; prophetic vision

scenes.caption: Prophetic vision · Ezekiel 37:9–10 · The wind and breath are suggested, not personified.

intro.title: The breath enters the vision
intro.note: This focused scene depicts Ezekiel 37:9–10: the prophet speaks to the wind, breath enters the bodies, and they stand. Dust and moving garments suggest wind without depicting a divine or humanlike figure. The image is a prophetic vision, not archaeological evidence or a resolution of disputed historical or resurrection readings.

hotspots.title: Ezekiel prophesies to the wind
hotspots.note: Ezekiel is told to prophesy to the wind and call for breath. The outstretched gesture and moving cloth suggest wind without portraying it as a being.

hotspots.title: The breath enters and the company stands
hotspots.note: The passage says the breath came into them, they lived, and stood on their feet as a great army. The clothed figures represent this moment in the prophet’s vision; no weaponry or battle is shown.

scenes.title: At dawn the king finds Daniel unharmed

art.alt: King Darius calls down to Daniel at dawn; Daniel stands unharmed among calm lions inside a generic stone den, literary reconstruction

scenes.caption: Literary reconstruction · Daniel 6:19–23 · No angel or divine figure is depicted.

intro.title: The king calls at dawn
intro.note: Daniel 6:19–23 recounts the king’s early visit to the lions’ den, his question to Daniel, and Daniel’s answer that he was unharmed. The image gathers the call and reply into one moment; it does not specify a known den or depict the angel Daniel mentions.

hotspots.title: Darius calls to Daniel at the den
hotspots.note: At dawn the king hurries to the den and calls to Daniel with concern. The stone opening is a literary reconstruction; no specific site is identified.

hotspots.title: Daniel answers, unharmed by the lions
hotspots.note: Daniel says God sent an angel who shut the lions’ mouths, and the text says he was found without injury. The angel is described in the note but not visualized.

scenes.title: The son’s name is given as a prophetic sign

art.alt: Hosea holds a newborn son while an adult woman and young daughter sit close by in a quiet courtyard; textual family sign, not a portrait

scenes.caption: Textual family sign · Hosea 1:8–9 · The episode’s historical or literary mode remains open.

intro.title: A son is born and named
intro.note: Hosea 1:8–9 reports the birth of another son after Lo-ruhamah is weaned and gives the name Lo-ammi as a sign of broken relationship. The family scene is a literary reconstruction, not a portrait, and does not settle the passage’s historical/literary mode. The image includes no written name.

hotspots.title: Another son is born after Lo-ruhamah is weaned
hotspots.note: The verse says Lo-ruhamah had been weaned and that Gomer then gave birth to another son. The older daughter and newborn appear together in the family scene.

hotspots.title: The child’s name carries the sign of separation
hotspots.note: The text names the son Lo-ammi and interprets the name as a sign that Israel is not the LORD’s people. The sign is stated in the text, not written into the image or placed on the child.

scenes.title: The vine and fig tree are laid waste

art.alt: An ancient farmer mourns beside a stripped vine and barked fig tree as locusts cross the ruined crop; literary reconstruction, no specific army or event identified

scenes.caption: Joel's locust imagery · Joel 1:7–12 · Literary reconstruction; no specific army or event asserted.

intro.title: A harvest is stripped
intro.note: Joel 1:7 pictures the vine laid waste and the fig tree stripped; verses 10–12 describe loss in field and orchard and the people's mourning. The locusts recall the oracle's earlier locust imagery (1:4), but the illustration does not identify them with a named army, date, or archaeological event.

hotspots.title: The vine and fig tree are stripped
hotspots.note: The verse says the vine is laid waste and the fig tree barked and stripped. The bare white branches and damaged vine visualize that description.

hotspots.title: The field and growers mourn the crop loss
hotspots.note: The passage says the field is wasted and the vine, fig, and other crops fail. The farmer is a visual representative of the mourning, not a named person in the text.

hotspots.title: Locusts cross the damaged crop
hotspots.note: The swarm recalls the successive locusts described earlier in the same oracle (1:4). It is a literary visualization and does not assert a specific army or historical identification.

scenes.title: A basket of summer fruit signals the end

art.alt: The prophet Amos studies a basket of ripe summer fruit beside a merchant weighing grain on a balance as a poor buyer waits; symbolic literary reconstruction

scenes.caption: Symbolic vision and social accusation · Amos 8:1–6 · Literary reconstruction, with no modern site asserted.

intro.title: Summer fruit and the announced end
intro.note: Amos 8:1–3 presents a basket of summer fruit as a sign of the announced end; the Hebrew wording plays on the sound of 'summer fruit' and 'end.' Verses 4–6 condemn merchants who cheat the poor. The market setting is a literary reconstruction joining two moments from the same oracle, not a claim about one historical place or exact event.

hotspots.title: Amos sees a basket of summer fruit
hotspots.note: Amos identifies what he sees as a basket of summer fruit; the LORD then says the end has come. The wordplay is in the text, not written on the fruit.

hotspots.title: The merchant’s weighing balance
hotspots.note: Amos 8:4–6 condemns dishonest measures and exploitation of the needy. The visible balance represents that accusation; the illustration cannot establish whether a particular weighing is dishonest.

hotspots.title: The needy wait while grain is weighed

art.alt: Jacob and Laban face one another beside a stone heap and upright pillar, with kin and a meal behind them; artistic reconstruction

scenes.caption: Illustrated reconstruction · Genesis 31:44–52

intro.title: A witness between them
intro.note: The selected scene brings the covenant, gathered heap, pillar and meal together. The memorial's arrangement, clothing, faces and highland view are illustrative; the image does not identify a surviving monument or exact ancient site.

hotspots.title: The heap is a witness
hotspots.note: Jacob's kin gather stones into a heap. Laban calls the heap a witness and says neither party is to pass it toward the other for harm.

hotspots.title: Jacob sets up a pillar
hotspots.note: Jacob takes a stone and sets it up as a pillar. Its upright shape here is illustrative rather than a record of the original memorial.

hotspots.title: The covenant between Jacob and Laban
hotspots.note: Laban proposes a covenant. The agreement includes concern for his daughters and a boundary against harm. The open-handed poses are an imagined way to depict their solemn exchange.

scenes.title: Jacob wrestles until the breaking of day

art.alt: Jacob and an unnamed man wrestle in a restrained standing clinch beside a river at dawn; artistic reconstruction

scenes.caption: Illustrated reconstruction · Genesis 32:24–30

intro.title: Jacob is named Israel
intro.note: The image selects the wrestling of verse 24 and uses ordinary human appearance for the figure the verse calls a man. It does not settle the encounter's theological identity: Jacob later names the place Peniel and says he has seen God face to face. Faces, clothing, stance and riverbank are illustrative; the exact site is not established.

hotspots.title: Jacob holds on
hotspots.note: Jacob is left alone and wrestles until daybreak. When told to let go, he says he will not do so unless he is blessed. The image avoids depicting the injury in verse 25.

hotspots.title: The man and the blessing
hotspots.note: The man asks Jacob's name, names him Israel, and blesses him. He does not supply his own name. Verse 30 records Jacob's words about seeing God; the illustration adds no halo, wings or divine portrait.

scenes.title: Jacob and Esau embrace
scenes.caption: Illustrated reconstruction · Genesis 33:1–4

intro.title: Reunion after separation
intro.note: The scene selects the brothers' embrace from Genesis 33:1–4. Human likenesses, clothing and the landscape are artistic interpretations.

hotspots.title: Esau embraces Jacob
hotspots.note: Esau runs to meet Jacob, embraces him, falls on his neck, kisses him, and they weep.

art.alt: Jacob and Esau weep in an embrace at the center of a warm rocky landscape; artistic reconstruction.

scenes.title: Jacob builds an altar at Bethel
scenes.caption: Illustrated reconstruction · Genesis 35:6–7

intro.title: An altar at Bethel
intro.note: This selected scene shows Jacob and the altar in Genesis 35:6–7. The altar form, kneeling pose, people and landscape are reconstructed; God is not pictured.

hotspots.title: Jacob at Bethel
hotspots.note: Jacob comes to Luz, also called Bethel, with the people accompanying him.

hotspots.title: The altar
hotspots.note: Jacob builds an altar and calls the place El-beth-el, remembering where God appeared to him when he fled from his brother.

art.alt: Jacob kneels beside a rough stone altar with a small encampment behind him; artistic reconstruction.

scenes.title: Joseph receives a distinctive coat
scenes.caption: Illustrated reconstruction · Genesis 37:3–4

intro.title: A coat and a father's favor
intro.note: The illustration selects Genesis 37:3–4. The KJV calls the garment a coat of many colours; its exact cut, weave and pattern are reconstructed. Faces, camp and poses are artistic interpretations.

hotspots.title: Joseph's coat
hotspots.note: Israel loves Joseph more than his other children and makes him a coat of many colours.

hotspots.title: The brothers' response
hotspots.note: The brothers see their father's special love for Joseph and hate him; they cannot speak peaceably to him. Their visible expressions are interpretive.

art.alt: Jacob presents Joseph with a richly colored woven coat while two brothers watch from the tent; artistic reconstruction.

scenes.title: The garment Joseph leaves behind
scenes.caption: Illustrated object study · Genesis 39:12–13 · Garment and setting reconstructed

intro.title: A garment left behind
intro.note: This object study refers to the garment Joseph leaves when he flees. Genesis does not describe its design or place it on a bench; the fabric, bench and courtyard are artistic staging. The encounter itself is not illustrated.

hotspots.title: The left garment
hotspots.note: Joseph leaves his garment in her hand and flees outside. The next verse again notes that he has left the garment and gone.

art.alt: A woven outer garment draped over a stone bench; interpretive object study of the garment Joseph left behind.

scenes.title: The cupbearer's dream
scenes.caption: Dream visualization · Genesis 40:9–11 · Artistic interpretation

intro.title: Grapes and Pharaoh's cup
intro.note: The chief butler tells Joseph a dream involving a vine, ripe grapes and Pharaoh's cup. This illustration visualizes that narrated dream alone; it does not depict a waking event or combine it with the baker's dream. Faces, objects and garden are interpretive.

hotspots.title: The vine and ripe grapes
hotspots.note: In the dream a vine stands before the cupbearer. Its three branches bud, blossom and bring forth ripe grapes. The image concentrates on the ripe grapes rather than proving a precise branch count.

hotspots.title: Grapes pressed into the cup
hotspots.note: The cupbearer takes the grapes, presses them into Pharaoh's cup and gives the cup to Pharaoh. The cup's form is reconstructed.

art.alt: The cupbearer squeezes grapes into a royal cup before a vine; artistic visualization of the narrated dream.

scenes.title: Pharaoh gives Joseph the ring
scenes.caption: Illustrated reconstruction · Genesis 41:42

intro.title: Joseph is clothed with authority
intro.note: Genesis 41:42 names Pharaoh's ring, fine linen and a gold neck chain. This scene selects the investiture; it does not combine the later gathering of grain into the same moment. Faces, regalia and palace details are artistic reconstruction.

hotspots.title: Pharaoh's ring
hotspots.note: Pharaoh takes his ring from his hand and puts it on Joseph's hand. Its exact design is reconstructed.

hotspots.title: Fine linen and a gold chain
hotspots.note: Joseph is arrayed in fine linen and given a gold chain about his neck. These visible objects are named in the verse; their styling is interpretive.

art.alt: Pharaoh places a ring on Joseph's hand; Joseph wears fine linen and a gold chain; artistic reconstruction.

scenes.title: Joseph's brothers bow before him
scenes.caption: Illustrated reconstruction · Genesis 42:6–8

intro.title: Recognized by Joseph
intro.note: Joseph sells food as governor. His brothers arrive from Canaan and bow before him; he recognizes them, but they do not recognize him. Faces, regalia, granary and staging are artistic reconstructions.

hotspots.title: The brothers bow
hotspots.note: Joseph's brothers come and bow before him with their faces to the earth.

hotspots.title: Joseph recognizes them
hotspots.note: Joseph recognizes his brothers and conceals his identity. Their failure to recognize him is part of the narrative, not something a still image can prove.

art.alt: Joseph sits as governor while his brothers bow with faces to the ground beside sacks of grain; artistic reconstruction.

scenes.title: Benjamin's larger portion
scenes.caption: Illustrated reconstruction · Genesis 43:31–34

intro.title: A meal with the brothers
intro.note: The selected meal episode includes separate dining arrangements and Benjamin's larger portion. Genesis says his portion was five times as much; the illustration signals abundance without serving as an exact measurement. People, food and dining furniture are reconstructed.

hotspots.title: Benjamin's portion
hotspots.note: Joseph sends portions from before him. Benjamin's portion is five times as much as any of the others, and they drink and are merry with him.

hotspots.title: Joseph eats separately
hotspots.note: The food is set for Joseph by himself, for the brothers by themselves, and for the Egyptians separately. The background table makes Joseph's separation visible.

art.alt: A large portion is served to Benjamin among his brothers; Joseph sits separately in the background; artistic reconstruction.

scenes.title: The silver cup in Benjamin's sack
scenes.caption: Illustrated object study · Genesis 44:1–2, 12–13

intro.title: A cup hidden and found
intro.note: Joseph orders the silver cup put in the youngest brother's sack. During the search it is found in Benjamin's sack. This object study links the placement and discovery rather than depicting every intervening action. Cup, money pieces, sack and roadside setting are reconstructed.

hotspots.title: Joseph's silver cup
hotspots.note: Joseph commands the steward to put his silver cup in the youngest brother's sack. The search later finds the cup in Benjamin's sack.

hotspots.title: Food and money in the sack
hotspots.note: The steward is told to fill the sacks with food and put every man's money in the sack's mouth. The plain metal pieces are interpretive; Genesis does not specify their shape.

art.alt: A silver cup sits visibly inside the open mouth of a grain sack beside plain money pieces; interpretive object study.

scenes.title: Joseph embraces Benjamin
scenes.caption: Illustrated reconstruction · Genesis 45:14–15

intro.title: Brothers reunited
intro.note: The scene selects the embrace after Joseph makes himself known. Joseph and Benjamin weep together; Joseph also kisses and weeps over his brothers before they speak with him. Human likenesses and room are artistic reconstruction.

hotspots.title: Joseph and Benjamin weep
hotspots.note: Joseph falls upon Benjamin's neck and weeps, and Benjamin weeps upon his neck.

hotspots.title: His brothers gather near
hotspots.note: Joseph kisses all his brothers and weeps upon them. Afterward they talk with him. The still image gathers them around the central embrace.

art.alt: Joseph embraces Benjamin and weeps, with his brothers gathered privately around them; artistic reconstruction.

scenes.title: Jacob's family travels in wagons
scenes.caption: Illustrated reconstruction · Genesis 46:5–7

intro.title: The household goes to Egypt
intro.note: Jacob's sons carry their father, wives and little ones in the wagons Pharaoh sent. They bring cattle, goods and the family into Egypt. This illustration does not identify an exact road or location; people, wagon forms and landscape are reconstructed.

hotspots.title: Jacob and the household in wagons
hotspots.note: The sons of Israel carry Jacob their father, their little ones and their wives in the wagons Pharaoh sent.

hotspots.title: Cattle and goods accompany them
hotspots.note: They take the cattle and goods acquired in Canaan and come into Egypt, with Jacob's descendants accompanying him.

art.alt: Elderly Jacob and family members ride in a wooden wagon among cattle and goods; artistic reconstruction of the family journey to Egypt.

scenes.title: Joseph supplies food in exchange for livestock
scenes.caption: Illustrated reconstruction · Genesis 47:15–17

intro.title: Food during the famine
intro.note: When money fails, the Egyptians ask Joseph for food. Joseph offers food in exchange for livestock. The selected scene makes Joseph visible in the transaction; his appearance, the people, grain sack and courtyard are reconstructed rather than a record of a specific exchange.

hotspots.title: Joseph supplies food
hotspots.note: The Egyptians come to Joseph when money fails. He tells them to bring their cattle, and he will give them food in exchange.

hotspots.title: Livestock exchanged for food
hotspots.note: Joseph gives food in exchange for horses, flocks, cattle and asses. The visible goat represents the flocks; one animal does not stand for an exact price or quantity.

art.alt: Joseph visibly gives a grain sack to an Egyptian man with a goat during the famine; artistic reconstruction.

scenes.title: Jacob crosses his hands to bless the boys
scenes.caption: Illustrated reconstruction · Genesis 48:13–16

intro.title: Ephraim and Manasseh are blessed
intro.note: Joseph brings his sons before Israel. Jacob places his right hand on younger Ephraim and his left on firstborn Manasseh, deliberately crossing his hands. The selected scene shows the blessing, with people, ages, clothing and room artistically reconstructed.

hotspots.title: Jacob deliberately crosses his hands
hotspots.note: Israel places his right hand upon Ephraim's head and his left upon Manasseh's, guiding his hands deliberately even though Manasseh is firstborn. Ephraim is shown at the viewer's right.

hotspots.title: The blessing of the lads
hotspots.note: Jacob calls on the God who fed him throughout his life and asks that the lads be blessed, bear the family name, and grow into a multitude. The invoked Angel is not pictured.

art.alt: Jacob crosses his arms to bless Ephraim and Manasseh, one hand on each boy's head; artistic reconstruction.

scenes.title: Judah compared to a lion
scenes.caption: Literary comparison · Genesis 49:9 · Symbolic illustration

intro.title: The lion in Jacob's words
intro.note: Jacob's blessing uses the lion as a poetic comparison for Judah. This symbol study visualizes the animal image in verse 9. It does not show a literal encounter, transformation, meeting or travel event, and it does not cover all the chapter's blessings. The landscape is interpretive.

hotspots.title: A lion as a comparison for Judah
hotspots.note: Jacob calls Judah a lion's whelp and describes him stooping and couching as a lion. The visible animal represents this literary comparison; Judah is not literally an animal in the narrative.

art.alt: A lion lies couched on warm rock; a symbolic illustration of Jacob's poetic comparison of Judah to a lion.

scenes.title: Joseph is placed in a coffin in Egypt
scenes.caption: Illustrated object study · Genesis 50:26 · Coffin form reconstructed

intro.title: Genesis closes in Egypt
intro.note: Genesis 50:26 says Joseph dies at 110, is embalmed, and is put in a coffin in Egypt. This respectful object study shows a closed coffin only. Its wooden rectangular form, room, platform and cloth are artistic reconstruction; no human remains are visible.

hotspots.title: The coffin in Egypt
hotspots.note: Joseph dies at the age of 110. He is embalmed and placed in a coffin in Egypt. The verse does not specify the coffin's exact design.

art.alt: A closed wooden coffin rests quietly in an Egyptian chamber, with no human remains visible; interpretive object study.

scenes.title: Families of Noah’s sons

scenes.caption: Diagram · Genesis 10:1–6, 21–22 · not geography, chronology, or a complete genealogy

intro.title: Selected families
intro.note: The branches show only names and relationships in the selected verses. They do not assign modern identities, boundaries, or dates.

hotspots.title: Noah and his sons
hotspots.note: The root and three son branches are visible in the diagram; the anchor is the passage that names the family.

hotspots.title: Japheth’s family
hotspots.note: The named sons of Japheth and selected Gomer/Javan descendants appear as text. The note for verse 5 avoids drawing borders or assigning modern peoples.

hotspots.title: Ham’s sons
hotspots.note: The four sons named in verse 6 are listed beneath Ham.

hotspots.title: Shem and his named children
hotspots.note: The diagram states the Eber-descendant relation in verse 21 separately and lists the children named in verse 22; it does not add intervening branches.

scenes.title: Names and a promised son
scenes.coverage: Genesis 17:5, 15, 19–21 · names and future promise only

art.alt: Text-only diagram linking Abram with Abraham, Sarai with Sarah, and identifying Isaac as promised for the future. No event or portrait.

scenes.caption: Diagram · Genesis 17:5, 15, 19–21 · not a map, timeline, birth scene, or full chapter

intro.title: Name changes and promise
intro.note: The passage gives new names and speaks of a future son; this diagram shows those textual links without picturing an event or implying the child is already born.

hotspots.title: Abram is named Abraham
hotspots.note: Both names and the name-giving reference are visible in the diagram.

hotspots.title: Sarai is named Sarah
hotspots.note: Both names and the name-giving reference are visible in the diagram.

hotspots.title: Isaac is promised to Sarah and Abraham
hotspots.note: Isaac is labeled as promised for the future, with the selected promise range. No birth scene is shown.

scenes.title: Family relationships and response

art.alt: Native text relationship guide showing Dinah as daughter of Jacob and Leah, Simeon and Levi as named brothers, and the closing exchange. No assault or retaliation is pictured.

scenes.caption: Relationship diagram · Genesis 34:1, 25, 30–31 · not a map, timeline, or full chapter; no assault or retaliation illustration

intro.title: Selected relationships
intro.note: The lines show only the family links named in the selected verses. The diagram addresses the chapter’s closing exchange without depicting or replacing its assault and retaliation.

hotspots.title: Dinah, daughter of Leah and Jacob
hotspots.note: The two parent links and Dinah’s name are visible; the relationship follows the selected verse.

hotspots.title: Simeon and Levi, Dinah’s brothers
hotspots.note: The text names the brothers and identifies them as Jacob’s sons; the diagram shows the sibling relationship without the violent act.

hotspots.title: Jacob and his sons’ exchange
hotspots.note: The diagram marks the response and reply as a text relationship; it does not illustrate the retaliation.

scenes.title: Esau and his named family

art.alt: Native text diagram identifying Esau as Edom and showing named wives and sons with explicitly stated maternal links; not geography, chronology, or the full chapter.

scenes.caption: Diagram · Genesis 36:1–5 · selected family, not a map, timeline, or full chapter

intro.title: A selected family profile
intro.note: The diagram stops at the names in verses 1–5 and shows mother-child links only where stated. It does not extend the genealogy into later verses.

hotspots.title: Esau, who is Edom
hotspots.note: The name Edom is associated with Esau in the selected verse.

hotspots.title: Esau’s named wives
hotspots.note: The three named wives are shown with their references; the diagram does not invent additional family details.

hotspots.title: Sons through the named mothers
hotspots.note: The diagram connects Eliphaz, Reuel, and the sons of Aholibamah to the mothers named in the selected verses.

scenes.title: The Hebrew midwives refuse the king

art.alt: Text sequence naming Shiphrah and Puah, their refusal to kill the children, Pharaoh’s questions, and the passage’s account of their households

scenes.caption: Editorial text diagram · Exodus 1:15–21

intro.title: The Hebrew midwives refuse the king
intro.note: This editorial diagram follows the named midwives and their response to the king. It shows text relationships rather than invented portraits or a reconstructed birth.

hotspots.title: Shiphrah and Puah
hotspots.note: Exodus 1:15 names the Hebrew midwives Shiphrah and Puah. The following verse gives the king’s command; this diagram does not depict harm to a child.

hotspots.title: The midwives keep the children alive
hotspots.note: The midwives fear God and do not carry out the king’s command. Exodus 1:17 explicitly says that they save the male children alive.

hotspots.title: Pharaoh questions the midwives
hotspots.note: The king asks why the male children have been kept alive, and the midwives answer him. The diagram identifies this exchange without inventing its setting.

hotspots.title: God deals well with the midwives
hotspots.note: The passage says that God deals well with the midwives and makes them houses because they fear God. “Houses” is retained as the text’s household language, not assigned to an invented building.

scenes.title: Moses is found among the reeds

art.alt: A clothed infant in an open woven basket among river reeds, Pharaoh’s daughter leaning toward him, an attendant, and his sister watching from nearby reeds

scenes.caption: Artistic reconstruction · Exodus 2:3–6

intro.title: Moses is found among the reeds
intro.note: The illustration gathers the basket, the watching sister, and the discovery described in Exodus 2:3–6 into one editorial composition. Their appearances, exact positions, and the riverbank are reconstructed, not known portraits or a mapped location.

hotspots.title: The basket among the reeds
hotspots.note: The child’s mother prepares an ark of bulrushes with slime and pitch and places it among the flags by the river’s brink. The hotspot identifies that basket; its open appearance belongs to the later discovery.

hotspots.title: His sister keeps watch
hotspots.note: Exodus 2:4 says that his sister stands afar off to learn what will happen. The girl is placed behind the reeds in this reconstructed scene; the illustration does not establish a precise distance.

hotspots.title: Pharaoh’s daughter has compassion
hotspots.note: Pharaoh’s daughter sees the basket, has it fetched, and opens it. When she sees the weeping child, she has compassion on him. The adult beside the open basket represents this response.

scenes.title: Moses at the burning bush

art.alt: A leafy bush surrounded by flame, barefoot Moses covering his face, and his removed sandals on a foreground rock in an imagined wilderness setting

scenes.caption: Artistic reconstruction · Exodus 3:2–6

intro.title: Moses at the burning bush
intro.note: The scene brings together the burning bush, the instruction about shoes, and Moses hiding his face. The bush is drawn with intact leaves. The landscape and Moses’s appearance are artistic reconstructions; God is not depicted as a human figure.

hotspots.title: The bush is not consumed
hotspots.note: Moses sees a bush burning with fire without being consumed and turns aside. God calls to him from the midst of the bush. The visible leafy branches identify the subject described in Exodus 3:2–4.

hotspots.title: Remove your shoes
hotspots.note: Exodus 3:5 commands Moses to remove his shoes because the ground on which he stands is holy. The sandals on the rock are an illustrative reconstruction of the shoes, not a recovered object.

hotspots.title: Moses hides his face
hotspots.note: After God identifies himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, Moses hides his face because he is afraid to look upon God. His covered face depicts the response stated in Exodus 3:6.

scenes.title: The rod becomes a serpent and a rod again

art.alt: Text diagram with three ordered states: a rod in Moses’s hand, a serpent on the ground, and a rod in his hand again

scenes.caption: Editorial text diagram · Exodus 4:2–4

intro.title: The rod becomes a serpent and a rod again
intro.note: This editorial sequence keeps three successive moments separate. It does not place a rod and serpent in one reconstructed instant, and it does not depict God.

hotspots.title: A rod in the hand
hotspots.note: When asked what is in his hand, Moses answers that it is a rod. This is the initial state of the sequence in Exodus 4:2.

hotspots.title: The rod becomes a serpent
hotspots.note: Moses casts the rod onto the ground. It becomes a serpent, and he flees from it, as stated in Exodus 4:3.

hotspots.title: A rod in the hand again
hotspots.note: Moses is told to take the serpent by the tail. When he takes it, it becomes a rod in his hand again. The diagram separates this outcome from the preceding moment.

scenes.title: Stubble is gathered while the brick quota remains

art.alt: Workers gather dry stubble beside a mudbrick yard with a wooden brick mould, rows of unfired bricks, and an overseer

scenes.caption: Artistic reconstruction · Exodus 5:10–13

intro.title: Stubble is gathered while the brick quota remains
intro.note: The painting combines nearby stubble gathering and brickmaking to explain the hardship in Exodus 5:10–13. The worksite, clothing, and appearances are reconstructed; it is not an identified archaeological site.

hotspots.title: Gather stubble for straw
hotspots.note: After the supply of straw is withheld, the people scatter to gather stubble instead of straw. The foreground gathering identifies the work described in Exodus 5:12.

hotspots.title: The daily brick quota remains
hotspots.note: The taskmasters tell the people to obtain their own straw while their work requirement is not reduced. They continue demanding the daily task. The mould and brick rows represent that unchanged burden.

scenes.title: The family line of Moses and Aaron

art.alt: Selected text genealogy linking Levi, his son Kohath, Kohath’s son Amram, and Amram and Jochebed’s sons Aaron and Moses

scenes.caption: Editorial text diagram · Exodus 6:16, 18, 20

intro.title: The family line of Moses and Aaron
intro.note: This selected genealogy uses only relationships named in Exodus 6:16, 18, and 20. It follows the line leading to Moses and Aaron; other descendants and the rest of the chapter remain in Scripture rather than being silently filled in.

hotspots.title: Levi and his named sons
hotspots.note: Exodus 6:16 names Gershon, Kohath, and Merari as Levi’s sons. The diagram follows the Kohath branch while retaining the other names in its label.

hotspots.title: Kohath and Amram
hotspots.note: Exodus 6:18 names Amram among Kohath’s sons. This relationship connects the selected generations without implying that the diagram shows every family branch.

hotspots.title: Aaron and Moses’s parents
hotspots.note: Exodus 6:20 names Amram and Jochebed and says that she bears Aaron and Moses. These names and their parental relationship are the subject of this node.

scenes.title: Rod sign before Pharaoh
scenes.caption: Editorial sequence diagram · Exodus 7:8–13 · selected events in order

art.alt: Three cards show Exodus 7:10–12 in order: Aaron casts down his rod, the Egyptian magicians cast down theirs, and Aaron’s rod swallows theirs. Green arrows mark the sequence; the events are not shown as one instant.

intro.title: The rod signs
intro.note: The diagram isolates Aaron’s action, the magicians’ imitation, and the swallowing in 7:10–12. The cards follow their narrated order; the forecast and Pharaoh’s response are not pictured.

hotspots.title: Aaron casts down the rod
hotspots.note: The sign is announced in 7:9 and carried out in 7:10.

hotspots.title: The magicians imitate the sign
hotspots.note: Exodus 7:11 describes the magicians doing in like manner with their enchantments. The following verse describes their rods becoming serpents and then Aaron’s rod swallowing theirs. The next diagram node follows that later event.

hotspots.title: Aaron’s rod swallows theirs
hotspots.note: The swallowing follows the magicians’ imitation; the two events are not simultaneous.

scenes.title: The river is struck and its water cannot be drunk

art.alt: Two men stand beside a crimson river, one holding a rod at the water, while an Egyptian ruler and attendants watch from the bank; artistic reconstruction

scenes.caption: Artistic reconstruction · Exodus 7:19–21

intro.title: The river is struck
intro.note: Exodus 7:19 gives the instruction about Egypt’s waters; verses 20–21 describe the river being struck, its water changing, and the consequences. This reconstructed riverbank combines those nearby moments. The figures, buildings, and location are illustrative.

hotspots.title: The river is struck with the rod
hotspots.note: Moses and Aaron carry out the instruction, and the river is struck with the rod before Pharaoh and his servants. The hotspot marks the rod meeting the changed water, as described in Exodus 7:20.

hotspots.title: Water that cannot be drunk
hotspots.note: Exodus 7:21 says that the fish die, the river stinks, and the Egyptians cannot drink its water. The foreground river identifies the affected water; its appearance and the riverbank are an artistic reconstruction.

scenes.title: Frogs are announced in the houses and cover the land

art.alt: Frogs gather in a kneading trough and across a mudbrick household floor and courtyard; an editorial illustration connecting the announced household detail and the sign covering the land

scenes.caption: Editorial composition · announcement and fulfillment · Exodus 8:1–6

intro.title: The frog sign
intro.note: This editorial composition connects the domestic locations announced in Exodus 8:3 with the frogs covering the land in Exodus 8:6. It is not one recorded instant. The household, trough, and frogs’ appearances are reconstructed; Aaron’s action over the waters is kept in Scripture rather than placed inside this house.

hotspots.title: Frogs in the kneading troughs
hotspots.note: Verse 8:3 announces that frogs will enter the houses, beds, ovens, and kneading troughs. The visible trough illustrates that announced domestic detail. It is distinct from the later statement that frogs cover the land.

hotspots.title: Frogs cover the land of Egypt
hotspots.note: After Aaron stretches his hand over the waters, Exodus 8:6 says that frogs come up and cover the land of Egypt. The frogs across the visible ground illustrate that outcome; this household setting is reconstructed.

scenes.title: Dust becomes lice; the magicians cannot reproduce the sign
scenes.caption: Editorial sequence diagram · Exodus 8:16–19 · action, failure, and speech in order

art.alt: Three cards follow Exodus 8:17–19: dust becomes lice after Aaron strikes it, the magicians cannot reproduce the sign, then they attribute it to God’s power. Green arrows mark the sequence. Their speech is shown as text; no hand is depicted.

intro.title: A sign they cannot reproduce
intro.note: The cards place the outcome at 8:17, the magicians’ failure at 8:18, and their words at 8:19. The final card reports speech; it does not depict a physical hand or Pharaoh’s response.

hotspots.title: Dust becomes lice
hotspots.note: Verse 8:16 gives the command; verse 8:17 describes the dust becoming lice.

hotspots.title: The magicians cannot do so
hotspots.note: The failed attempt is in 8:18; 8:19 records the magicians’ following speech.

hotspots.title: The finger of God
hotspots.note: This phrase is the magicians’ recorded speech. No hand or Pharaoh response is shown.

scenes.title: Swarms and Goshen’s announced distinction
scenes.caption: Editorial comparison · Exodus 8:20–24 · a reported outcome beside an announcement

art.alt: Two text panels compare Exodus 8:20–24: verse 24 reports swarms in Pharaoh’s and his servants’ houses and in Egypt; verses 22–23 announce a distinction for Goshen. The panels show neither a map nor a separately observed Goshen outcome.

intro.title: A reported swarm and a Goshen announcement
intro.note: Verses 8:22–23 announce that no swarms will be in Goshen. Verse 8:24 reports the swarms in Pharaoh’s and his servants’ houses and across Egypt. This comparison does not state that 8:24 separately observes Goshen without flies and does not add a map boundary.

hotspots.title: Swarms enter the houses
hotspots.note: Verse 8:21 announces the swarms; verse 8:24 reports them in Pharaoh’s and his servants’ houses and across Egypt.

hotspots.title: Goshen is set apart
hotspots.note: The distinction is announced in 8:22–23, before the swarm outcome is reported at 8:24. No later observation for Goshen is claimed.
